title: How would you store and query time-series data at scale?
summary: Time-series data has a distinct shape — append-only, time-ranged, and eager to shrink with age. Learn to design for it instead of treating it like generic relational rows.

slides.markdown:
Metrics, sensor readings, and event logs share a shape that makes them a different design problem from generic relational data: writes are append-only and arrive continuously, queries are almost always scoped to a time range, and fine-grained history matters far less the older it gets.

Treating this like an ordinary table — insert rows, index a few columns, keep everything forever — works until volume makes it collapse. This topic walks the actual design levers: time-based partitioning, downsampling, and picking a store built for this shape.

Ask: **what's the write rate, the retention period, and the typical query — a single point, or a range and aggregate?** A system ingesting a million points per second at 1-second resolution has fundamentally different storage needs from one ingesting a handful per minute.

Also ask how far back queries typically need full resolution versus a rough trend — this directly determines how aggressively you can downsample older data without losing anything anyone actually uses.

Structure it as: **partition by time range, write append-only, downsample old data instead of keeping full resolution forever.** These three levers together define most production time-series designs, regardless of the specific database chosen.

"I'd partition storage by time window so a query for 'the last hour' never touches older data. Writes only ever append new points, never update existing ones. And I'd downsample data past a defined age — full resolution for recent data, progressively coarser for older data — so storage doesn't grow unbounded."

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a downsampling schedule for ingested metrics
slides.markdown:
A concrete retention and downsampling policy for metrics ingested at 1-second resolution:

```
0 - 24 hours:    1-second resolution   (raw, full detail)
1 - 30 days:     1-minute resolution   (60x reduction)
30+ days:        1-hour resolution     (3600x reduction from raw)
```

A background job rolls up older data into coarser buckets on a schedule, then the original fine-grained points past their window can be deleted, since the data volume savings only materialize once the raw points are actually removed, not just once the rollup exists alongside them.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a purpose-built store vs a generic relational table
slides.markdown:
| | Generic relational table | Time-series / wide-column store |
|---|---|---|
| Write pattern | Optimized for scattered updates | Optimized for high-throughput append-only writes |
| Storage | Row-oriented, no native downsampling | Column-oriented compression, built-in rollup support |
| Time-range queries | Requires manual indexing and partitioning | Time-range scans are a first-class, optimized operation |
| Retention | Manual deletion jobs | Native TTL and retention policies |

**How to decide:** at meaningful scale, a purpose-built store (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, a wide-column store like Cassandra) does natively what you'd otherwise hand-build on top of a generic relational table.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a query hitting the right resolution tier
slides.markdown:
A query for "the last 24 hours at 1-second resolution" hits the hot tier directly:

```
SELECT * FROM metrics_raw
WHERE ts > now() - interval '24 hours';
```

A query for "the last year, at whatever resolution is available" hits the rolled-up tier instead, since that's all that still exists that far back:

```
SELECT * FROM metrics_hourly
WHERE ts > now() - interval '1 year';
```

The application or query layer needs to know which tier serves which time range — often abstracted behind a single query interface that routes internally, so callers don't have to know the retention policy themselves.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Say this explicitly: **downsampling cuts storage hard, but permanently discards fine-grained history — decide upfront what resolution you'll actually need later, because you can't reconstruct it after the raw points are gone.** This is a one-way decision at the point old raw data is deleted.

A candidate who names this permanence, and asks what resolution stakeholders will actually need a year from now before finalizing the retention policy, is showing real judgment — not just implementing a rollup because it saves space.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: full resolution needed from six months ago
slides.markdown:
If the retention policy already rolled that data up and deleted the raw points, the honest answer is: no, that data is gone, and this is exactly the permanence the trade-off warned about. This is why the resolution schedule needs sign-off from whoever actually needs incident-review-grade data, before it's finalized — not decided unilaterally by whoever's optimizing storage cost.

A mitigation worth naming: keep raw data slightly longer for known-sensitive systems (payment processing, safety-critical sensors) even if the general policy downsamples faster elsewhere, rather than applying one retention policy uniformly regardless of what's at stake for different data.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: handling a burst of out-of-order data
slides.markdown:
Time-series systems need an explicit **acceptance window** — how far back a late-arriving point can still be written before it's rejected or handled specially. A point arriving 30 seconds late for an already-closed 1-minute bucket either needs that bucket to be reopened and recomputed, or the late point gets routed to a separate correction path.

Name the choice: reopening buckets is more correct but adds complexity to every downstream rollup that already ran on the old value; rejecting or side-channeling late points is simpler but means the primary data is knowingly incomplete for a window after ingestion.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: storing raw time-series data forever in a generic table
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We'll just store every metric point at full resolution forever in our regular relational database — storage is cheap."

**Why it's wrong:** storage cost isn't the only cost — query performance degrades as the table grows unbounded, since a generic relational table has no built-in notion of rolling up or expiring old data, and every query scanning a time range pays the cost of the entire accumulated history sitting alongside it.

**Correct model:** downsample or expire data past a defined age, and use a store with native time-range and retention support once volume justifies it — full-resolution-forever is rarely the right default at real scale.

"I'd partition storage by time range so range queries stay cheap, write append-only since time-series data is rarely updated in place, and downsample older data instead of keeping full resolution forever — recent data stays fine-grained, older data gets progressively coarser. I'd use a purpose-built time-series or wide-column store once volume justifies it, since it gives this natively instead of hand-built on a generic table. And I'd name the trade-off explicitly: downsampling is a one-way door, so the retention schedule needs real sign-off before old raw data is deleted for good."
